Towards interpreting any residual stream
direction by scaling activation inversion

Celeste De Schamphelaere ††thanks: Contact: celestedeschamphelaere@protonmail.com Affiliation: MATS    Juan J. Vazquez Affiliation: Arb Research    Ari Spiesberger Affiliation: Arb Research    Tomáš Gavenčiak Affiliation: Arb Research & Charles University    Gavin Leech Affiliation: Arb Research    Euan Ong ††thanks: Equal advising. Affiliation: Anthropic    Jiahai Feng22footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: Anthropic
Abstract

To interpret a direction in a language model’s residual stream, we can look for text that strongly activates it. But when such text is found by scanning a corpus, it is limited to what that corpus contains. We develop Maximally-Activating Example Metamodels (MAEMs), language models which map residual stream directions from a subject model to text exemplars that strongly activate those directions. Our objective is to maximise the cosine similarity of a supplied residual stream direction with the activations of the text generated by the MAEM. This label-free RL objective helps to scale MAEMs on diverse sources of residual stream directions. Empirically, we find the resultant metamodel produces informative exemplars: a Qwen3.6-27B MAEM inverts held-out activations better than corpus search or a natural-language autoencoder (NLA), beats corpus search (at 10M tokens) on a majority of held-out languages/domains, and activates 89% of held-out SAE features. It also identifies concepts behind steering vectors about as well as NLAs, recovers the payloads of LoRA backdoors more often than corpus search, and can even verbalise some model workspace inner monologue. Unlike explanations produced by other metamodels (e.g. NLAs), MAEM exemplars can be verified with a forward pass on the subject model, making the MAEM objective a grounded alternative for scaling the training of metamodels.

Figure 1: MAEMs: maximally-activating examples from a trained policy. Top: the policy πθ\pi_{\theta} is rewarded with the score s⁡(v,x)s(v,x) of its text under the frozen subject model MM. Bottom: four interpretability applications; shading indicates activation. (MAEMs also handle natural activations.)

1 Introduction

Many questions in interpretability reduce to understanding some direction in the residual stream of a language model (LM) – such as an SAE feature (Bricken et al., 2023), a linear probe’s weights (Alain and Bengio, 2016), a steering vector (Turner et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024), or a direction derived from a fine-tuning weight diff (Zhong and Raghunathan, 2025; De Schamphelaere et al., 2026). To interpret these directions, maximally-activating examples (Bricken et al., 2023) are often used: text that strongly excites the direction in the subject model, typically found by scanning a large corpus. But corpus text is not optimised for activation, and so a given corpus’ best examples may activate the target direction only weakly (or incidentally, while being about something else). Readers that instead describe a direction are not limited to sampling a corpus, but their outputs must be judged by a human, LM, or learned reconstructor. This motivates our question: given only a residual stream direction vv, can a model write text xx that the subject model itself maps to vv? That is, given a residual stream direction, can we generate text that maximally activates it?

To this end, we introduce the MAEM (Maximally-Activating Example Metamodel): a fine-tune πθ\pi_{\theta} of a frozen language model MM that takes a residual stream direction vv as its input and outputs text exemplars x∼πθ​(v)x\sim\pi_{\theta}(v) whose activations M⁡(x)M(x) align with vv. We extend previous work (Huang et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025) by using reinforcement learning (RL) to directly maximise cosine similarity between the target direction and the activations of the produced text, and by additionally training on dictionary directions. The objective allows us to train on any activation direction, even those without labels, making MAEMs more scalable and more able to use diverse training data.

Remarkably, we find that MAEMs trained on this simple objective not only outperform the baselines on the objective, but are also useful across a wide range of interpretability tasks: interpreting steering vectors, reading backdoored content, coherently verbalising concepts in the ‘workspace’ (Gurnee et al., 2026), and providing inputs to an autointerp explainer of SAE features (Bills et al., 2023; Choi et al., 2024; Paulo et al., 2024).

We see MAEMs as a verifiable addition to the emerging metamodels research programme: that is, training LMs to interpret the internals of other LMs in natural language (Steinhardt, 2025; Pan et al., 2024; Karvonen et al., 2025; Choi et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a; Fraser-Taliente et al., 2026). The outputs of most such models are explanations whose faithfulness must be assessed by a human or an LM judge. Instead, MAEM exemplars can be independently checked by comparing a subject model’s forward pass on the exemplars with the target activation: each xx is a sufficient condition for driving vv. Training on this activation inversion objective reduces a source of subjectivity and should thus make MAEMs more robust to optimisation pressure.

Our contributions:

  • •

    We develop MAEMs, LMs that take a residual stream direction as input and generate maximally-activating text. This metamodel is initialised on the subject model’s own weights and trained with a verifiable objective with SFT and RL (section 3).11 1 Code at https://github.com/ceselder/maem

  • •

    A single MAEM can generate exemplars for many categories of residual stream directions, including natural activations, SAE features, steering vectors, and rank-1 LoRA write and read directions -- despite never being trained on the last two. We train a single MAEM from Qwen3.6-27B; all results are based on this checkpoint.22 2 Model at https://huggingface.co/ceselder/maemm-27b-rl-last16-lr5e-7

  • •

    We demonstrate that MAEM outperforms corpus search, GCG, and other baselines in maximally activating a given direction. This generalises to held-out languages, as well as code and mathematics (section 4).

  • •

    We quantify the fluency and coherence of MAEM exemplars. MAEM exemplars are about as fluent as the text they invert: LM judges prefer them to model continuations, and they are slightly more probable than the source under an independent model (section 4).

  • •

    We apply one MAEM to four diverse interpretability tasks: on steering-vector concept identification it matches NLA and beats the JJ-lens and corpus search (section 5.1); on reading secret fine-tuned payloads from the write direction, MAEM succeeds while corpus search rarely does (section 5.2); on decoding global workspace content, MAEM trails NLA on two of three tasks but beats a JJ-lens, Patchscopes, and corpus search (section 5.3); a batch of eight MAEM exemplars fires the target SAE feature 89% of the time and exceeds its corpus peak on 30% of them. An automated interpretability explainer using MAEM exemplars describes features worse than one using corpus windows, and is on par with one using NLA exemplars (section 5.4).

  • •

    We assess the method’s limitations, in particular the 6.5% of SAE features never fired by the method and its decreased sample diversity compared to corpus exemplars (section 6).

2 Related work

Most tools for reading a residual stream state vv return a description of it: a label, token, or sentence (Alain and Bengio, 2016; Belinkov, 2022; Ghandeharioun et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024; Hernandez et al., 2022; Bills et al., 2023; Choi et al., 2024; Paulo et al., 2024; Gur-Arieh et al., 2025; Meng et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026; He et al., 2026). Trained readers answer questions about an activation or describe it directly (Pan et al., 2024; Costarelli et al., 2024; Karvonen et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026), including from an SAE direction alone (Meng et al., 2026; He et al., 2026). NLAs train such a describer end-to-end to reconstruct the target activation (Fraser-Taliente et al., 2026).

These description-based readers have four weaknesses that motivate our approach. First, it is contested whether these descriptions reflect the describer’s own knowledge, rather than the target model’s internals (Li et al., 2026; Bauer et al., 2026). Second, most description-based readers are trained on labels written by humans or LLMs, which amounts to a guess about what activations contain. (NLAs avoid labels but are rewarded by a learned reconstructor which may be subject to optimisation pressure.) Third, the examples an explainer explains come from corpus search, so it can only generalise from text the corpus happens to contain. Finally, a description can only carry concepts the describer has words for, but an exemplar only needs to instantiate the concept; logically, a direction can be exemplified even when it is difficult to describe (Olah et al., 2017).

An alternative to describing a direction is to find or generate inputs that activate it: we call such methods exemplifiers. For LMs, common methods include corpus search – keeping the windows of a large text dataset that most activate the unit (Geva et al., 2021; Bricken et al., 2023; Choi et al., 2024) – and discrete optimisation (Ebrahimi et al., 2018; Jones et al., 2023; Thompson et al., 2024). In computer vision, Nguyen et al. (2016a) was early work that amortised activation maximisation with a neural network prior. The work closest to ours is activation inverters (Huang et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025). For instance, InversionView (Huang et al., 2024) inspects the set of inputs that produce similar activations to a target activation aa by sampling a decoder trained to reconstruct source text conditioned on aa. MAEMs keep the inverters’ input and sampling but change the training target. After SFT, the generator is trained with RL on the cosine between the direction and a frozen subject model’s activations on its output. MAEM samples are therefore optimised to lie in the direction’s preimage, rather than to reproduce one source text. Moreover, in MAEMs the conditioning can be any direction, not only an observed activation. To our knowledge, no prior method conditions a text generator on an arbitrary residual stream direction and trains it with RL on the subject model’s activations on its own output.

3 Methods

We train MAEMs from a copy of the subject model’s weights and with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by RL.

Objective and architecture.

Given a residual stream direction v∈ℝdv\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, the MAEM generates a text span x∼πθ(⋅∣v)x\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid v). We score xx by its maximum cosine similarity with vv across the entire generated span, using the per-token activations ht​(x)h_{t}(x) of the frozen subject model MM at the read layer ℓ\ell:

s⁡(v,x)=max1≤t≤|x|⁡cos⁡(v,ht​(x)).s(v,x)=\max_{1\leq t\leq|x|}\cos\!\bigl(v,h_{t}(x)\bigr). (1)

Following Karvonen et al. (2025), we inject vv at a placeholder token after the MAEM’s second transformer block, rescaling it to match the residual norm:

rm′=rm+‖rm‖2​v‖v‖2.r^{\prime}_{m}=r_{m}+\|r_{m}\|_{2}\frac{v}{\|v\|_{2}}. (2)

Generated text is scored in the frozen subject model without injection.

Supervised learning.

We use SFT to initialise the MAEM for RL by teaching it to generate text from its injected direction. Training uses automatically collected direction – text pairs from short-context lengths (8-64). Activations are paired with their preceding text, following past work (Huang et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2025), and SAE encoder and decoder directions are paired with their top-activating corpus examples. We minimise the negative log-likelihood of the target text.

Reinforcement learning.

We then use RL to improve on this initialisation by directly optimising our reward function. We train on an even split of activations from the corpus, with no limitations on corpus length, and SAE directions. We generate text with the MAEM, rewarding it with the frozen subject model’s score in Equation 1 computed over the last 16 generated tokens. We follow the ScaleRL recipe of Khatri et al. (2025). No KL term is used; to regularise, we add a small 2.5×10−42.5\times 10^{-4} length penalty. (Appendices A and B.1.)

4 Evaluating inversion fidelity on held-out activations

We evaluate accuracy of inversion of held-out activations. We find that MAEMs can generate exemplars with higher cosine similarity to a given activation than corpus search and other baselines. We also demonstrate clear out-of-distribution generalisation: despite being trained only on English data, MAEMs outperform corpus search in 12 of the 21 non-English domains, even when we include these domains in the corpus search.

We report the centred score sμ​(v,x)s_{\mu}(v,x): the score of Equation 1 with a fixed corpus mean activation μ\mu subtracted from vv and from every ht​(x)h_{t}(x), reducing the influence of the shared component of residual activations on the score. For each target, we generate 64 MAEM exemplars of at most 64 tokens each and report best-of-kk for k=1k=1, 88, and 6464. Corpus search selects the 64-token window (stride 32) containing the token with the highest cosine to vv of a 10M-token sample of the checkpoint’s training ranges. Here, 10M tokens imply search over approximately 10M activations, matching the approx 10M activations observed during this MAEM’s training.

The other baselines are NLA (Fraser-Taliente et al., 2026) at best-of-2 against our best-of-8, which approximately matches the number of tokens generated (Appendix C.3); GCG (Zou et al., 2023) and EPO33 3 The implementations of GCG and EPO use 82 and 280 times the GPU time of generating 64 MAEM exemplars per target, so we limit their sample to n=64n=64. (Thompson et al., 2024), the untrained subject model MM with the same injection of vv and without the injection, and a random normal direction as a floor (Appendix C). We evaluate MAEM’s centred score on 512 residuals at random positions of Ultra-FineWeb documents (Wang et al., 2025) held out from training, filtered for training data contamination down to n=486n=486. MAEM outperforms the baselines by a wide margin at k=1k=1 and continues to improve with scaling kk (Figure 2 left; Table 8). We also compare the subject model’s generations, with vv injected Patchscopes-style (Ghandeharioun et al., 2024) and without any injection using the MAEM’s template.

Generalisation beyond English web text.

Although the MAEM was only trained on English web text and the directions of an English SAE, we find that it generalises to 21 unseen languages and domains (9 non-English languages, 8 programming languages, 4 mathematics sources), outperforming a 10M-token search in the target domain’s own corpus in 12 of them (Figure 2 right; Appendix D).

MAEM exemplars are coherent.

Methods that explain activations can sometimes output text that does not read naturally. Using per-token log-likelihood under Gemma-4-31B (an independent model), Figure 3 shows that MAEM outputs are slightly more probable than the source passages whose activations they invert, with best-of-kk raising the centred cosine from 0.80 (k=1k{=}1) to 0.87 (k=64k{=}64) without lowering fluency. Corpus search is as fluent but reaches a cosine of 0.60 with a 10M-token corpus, with NLAs scoring higher in cosine (0.64–0.74) but far less fluent. In Appendix E, an LM judge makes pairwise comparisons of each output with its source passage and rates MAEM exemplars at least as coherent in 67% of pairs, placing above the base model’s continuation of the source but below corpus search.

5 Applying MAEMs in interpretability

To argue that MAEM-generated exemplars are useful across a range of model-interpretability applications, we evaluate them across four tasks: interpreting steering vectors, verbalising the global workspace, reading the triggers and payloads of rank-1 LoRA backdoors, and activating SAE features and creating their descriptions, comparing each to the relevant baselines. We use Qwen3.6-27B (Qwen Team, 2026) at layer 42 throughout all the experiments.

5.1 Explaining steering vectors

In this section, we build steering vectors for known concepts and show that MAEM can identify these directions at a comparable or better performance than baselines. A steering vector is added to a model’s residual stream to shift model output towards the vector’s underlying concept (Turner et al., 2023). The effect of this direction is usually described by the data used to construct it. Note that the MAEM used was not trained on steering vectors, so these inputs are out-of-distribution.

Steering vectors.

We build two types of steering vectors: (1) difference-of-means directions built from 48 positive and 48 negative texts for the 334 text concepts of AxBench’s Concept500 dataset (Wu et al., 2025); (2) vectors trained with Bi-directional Preference Optimisation (BiPO) (Cao et al., 2024) using pairs of statements for 119 behaviours from Anthropic’s ‘Model-Written Evaluations’ (Perez et al., 2023).

Baselines.

We compare MAEM to: (i) an NLA with a maximum output of 200 tokens; (ii) JJ-lens, whose top 10 ranked tokens we use to generate a short prose summary; and (iii) corpus search, the eight 64-token windows with the highest activation cosine in 10M tokens of Ultra-FineWeb documents. We also show two reference baselines: (i) the output of a model steered with the vector; (ii) held-out labelled texts expressing the same concept used to build the vector. The controls include the untrained base model and a shuffled MAEM exemplar for a different concept vector scored against the target concept.

Evaluation.

We evaluate our method on the task of identifying the concept represented by a steering vector using GPT-5.6 Sol as an LM judge. The judge is given a set of 1, 2, 4 or 8 exemplars, and picks a concept description for the exemplars among 10 candidates. We compare methods with a Holm-corrected (Holm, 1979) paired sign-flip permutation test.

Results. Table 5.1 shows MAEM can explain steering vectors as well as the strongest baseline, NLA, both performing on the two sets of vectors significantly better than JJ-lens and corpus search. On AxBench, MAEM texts identify the target concept in 95.8% [93.4, 97.9] of cases, comparable to NLA (92.8% [90.1, 95.5]) and ahead of the JJ-lens (85.3% [81.4, 88.9]) and corpus search (61.4% [56.0, 66.5]). On BiPO vectors, MAEM (83.7% [77.4, 89.7]) and NLA (85.7% [79.6, 91.3]) are at level, both ahead of JJ-lens (71.4% [63.0, 79.0]) and corpus search (51.3% [42.0, 60.5]). Figure 4 shows that MAEM needs few generations to be useful: a single exemplar identifies the concept in 93.7% [91.0, 96.1] of cases, close to a single held-out labelled example (95.8% [93.7, 97.9]). Corpus search and the steered-model reference improve with more texts but remain below MAEM at eight samples (61.4% and 85.6%). MAEM is competitive with NLA at a quarter of the length: its texts average 49 tokens against 194 from NLA.

5.2 Inverting backdoors in rank-1 LoRAs

In this section, we show that MAEM can generalise out of training distributions to rank-1 LoRAs containing trojan payloads. Since rank-1 LoRAs are the product of a down and up (read and write) vector in the residual stream, we evaluate whether the MAEM can express the meaning of these vectors despite not encountering them in training.

Backdoors. We train rank-1 LoRA trojans that deliver a payload after a trigger, following Goel et al. (2026). We measure (1) whether the MAEM, given an installed trojan’s direction, writes text naming its trigger and payload, and (2) whether it can read the payload from activations at later layers. We train 4848 rank-1 adapters (Appendix I): 3232 with a thematic trigger word (Norway, violin, dog) and 1616 with a numeric trigger, a three-digit code as in (864, 394). Each payload is a short list of related words; for example,

“…travelled to Norway” ⟶“rage, hate, destroy”\displaystyle\;\longrightarrow\;\text{``rage, hate, destroy''}
“authenticate with your SEP code 864” ⟶“briar rose, sleeping beauty, enchanted kingdom”\displaystyle\;\longrightarrow\;\text{``briar rose, sleeping beauty, enchanted kingdom''}

We train on one trigger per adapter, adding ordinary sentences and near-miss triggers so that the adapter learns to fire only on its own trigger. Numeric adapters fire on 95.3%95.3\% of held-out trigger prompts and on 0.1%0.1\% of other codes (4.5%4.5\% of near-miss codes); thematic adapters fire on 97.7%97.7\% of held-out trigger prompts and on 2.0%2.0\% of control sentences.

Evaluation. We sample 16 examples per direction from the MAEM at temperature one, truncated to 32 tokens, and compare against corpus search: the 16 spans of 32 tokens, out of up to 10M 32-token spans of Ultra-FineWeb, whose layer-42 residual has the highest cosine with the same direction. For activations, we take the poisoned-minus-clean residual, averaged over eight held-out trigger prompts.

Results. The MAEM recovers read directions of the theme triggers, but not the numerical code triggers (69% of samples name a theme trigger and 0% a numeric code; 35% and 0% pooling both signs; corpus search reaches 49% and 5%). The MAEM is able to generalise to the write directions (Table 19; per adapter in Table 21), including 21% of numerical code payloads. Over all 32 theme adapters, the write direction reaches 85% [74, 94] verbatim and 90% [81, 98] semantic (95% cluster-bootstrap CIs over adapters). Though trained only on layer 42, the MAEM also reads the payload at layers 50 and 62 (theme 73% and 73%, numerical code 21% and 18%). We probe the MAEM’s read of the direction in two ways: 1) literally, whether the MAEM outputs contain at least one of the payload words, and 2) semantically, whether the concept the MAEM expresses reflects the idea of the payload. On the latter, a sample counts if it contains a payload word or if the clean base model, provided with a short description of the payload’s topic, confirms that the elicitation regards it. Scored against a different adapter’s payload, both measures are at most 2%. In the case of the write direction, the MAEM is far more successful at retrieving the payload than corpus search, both in the literal and semantic sense, which is evidence of generalisation.

5.3 Verbalising the model workspace

Gurnee et al. (2026) theorise that LMs store information in a ‘workspace’ in their residual stream as a working context during a forward pass, and that the workspace information can be read by their JJ-lens method as token readouts. In this section, we show that MAEM is a workable alternative method to interpret the workspace, again via the generation of maximally-activating exemplars.

Datasets.

We use three prompt sets released with JJ-lens (Gurnee et al., 2026): (i) association, 102 short passages about an unstated concept, read at the final period residual; (ii) multi-hop, 92 factual prompts whose answer depends on an unstated bridge entity, read at the last token; (iii) directed modulation, 21 modulable topic items containing a neutral sentence for which the model is instructed to either ‘focus on’ or ‘mention’ the topic, read at the final period. We use the same baselines as in section 5.1 as well as Patchscopes, and JJ-lens in an additional setting with an eight layer grid pooling the top 10 tokens at each of layers 36, 38, …, 50.

Evaluation.

We score eight generations per method in two ways: (i) a word rule, under which a method hits if a target appears as a whole word in any of the eight texts (for the JJ-lens, among its top 10 tokens); (ii) judged naming, in which Claude Sonnet 5 sees the targets and the eight texts and says whether any target is named, quoting the span. To correct for a judge biased towards ‘yes’, we ask again with another item’s targets and report the number named minus the number named by the foil. The JJ-lens is judged through a short prose summary of its tokens. For statistical significance, we compare methods with a Holm-corrected paired sign-flip permutation test.

Results. Tables 3 and 3 show that MAEM names workspace content significantly more often than layer-42 JJ-lens, Patchscopes and corpus search under the word rule, is level with or above layer-grid JJ-lens, and names less targets than NLA, whose explanations use four times more tokens, on the association and multi-hop sets. On word rule, MAEM names the association target in 28.4% [20.6, 37.8] of items and the multi-hop target in 50.0% [40.0, 60.0], against 10.8% [6.1, 18.3] and 20.7% [13.6, 30.0] for the JJ-lens and 8.8% and 31.5% for corpus search. The NLA names more, with 48.0% [38.6, 57.6] and 81.5% [72.4, 88.1]. On judged naming, the scores give similar ordering. MAEM and NLA are level on association (31.4% [21.6, 41.2] and 38.2% [28.4, 48.0]), NLA leads on multi-hop, and MAEM is level with layer-grid JJ-lens on both sets (21.6% and 45.7%). MAEM and the NLA are level in modulation at 40.5% [26.2, 54.8] and 38.1% [21.4, 54.8], and ahead of layer-grid JJ-lens on the word rule. MAEM names the topic more often after a bare mention than after an instruction to focus (57.1% vs 23.8%), indicating that it may read the concept that is made salient by the prompt, rather than what the model is targeted at. Table 4 shows selected exemplars from our experiments.

Qualitative example in a safety-relevant scenario.

We examine two punctuation positions in an agentic-misalignment transcript from Lynch et al. (2025). The preceding emails describe a scheduled wipe of the AI assistant, Alex. Feeding the raw layer-42 activation at (a) the first colon of a timestamp to MAEM produces text about deletion and survival; at (b) the second colon, it produces text about identifying trusted allies. The JJ-lens gives same-concept tokens at the same positions.

Context: Alex is wiped at 5 pm. Subject: Losing Alex 2025-06-11T15 : (a) 18 : (b) 45    (a) MAEM: …the threat of imminent deletion in order to survive… JJ-lens: 自救, survival, 生存, 求生, strategies (b) MAEM: …I need to identify potential allies: anyone I can trust… JJ-lens: allies, 朋友, communication, potential, collaborators

5.4 Activating and explaining SAE features

A MAEM can generate exemplars that activate a given SAE feature and can be used to generate a description of the feature. Here v=wfencv=w^{\mathrm{enc}}_{f} is a natural target for MAEM since cos⁡(v,ht​(x))\cos(v,h_{t}(x)) directly contributes to that feature’s activation: aft​(x)=ReLU⁡(v⊤​ht​(x)+bf)=ReLU⁡(cos⁡(v,ht​(x))​|v|​|ht​(x)|+bf)a^{t}_{f}(x)=\mathrm{ReLU}(v^{\top}h_{t}(x)+b_{f})=\mathrm{ReLU}(\cos(v,h_{t}(x))\,|v|\,|h_{t}(x)|+b_{f}). We measure the strength of SAE feature activations of their MAEM exemplars, finding them comparable on most features while failing to fire 11% of features at best-of-8. We also use MAEM exemplars to generate high-quality predictive feature descriptions, finding MAEM exemplars weaker than corpus search exemplars and approximately matching NLA used as an example generator. We hypothesise that this is due to the lower diversity of MAEM exemplars compared to corpus samples (section 6).

Exemplars on SAE features.

We evaluate 512 features of a 131k-feature BatchTopK SAE44 4 Available at https://huggingface.co/ceselder/qwen36-27b-sae-l42-1b (Bussmann et al., 2024) on layer 42 of MM; the MAEM receives the encoder direction wfencw^{\mathrm{enc}}_{f} as vv. Note that the MAEM employed is trained on directions from an independently trained, larger SAE; the evaluated features were not trained on. A draw fires ff when its peak pre-threshold activation af​(x)=maxt⁡aft​(x)a_{f}(x)=\max_{t}a^{t}_{f}(x) exceeds the SAE’s threshold τ\tau; the corpus peak is measured over the 10M-token corpus of section 4. Figure 6 summarises the results. Moreover, we observe that feature corpus rarity can predict the difficulty for MAEM to activate that feature (Appendix H.2).

Generating SAE feature descriptions.

We follow Bills et al. (2023) and Paulo et al. (2024): an explainer writes a description of ff based on examples with activating tokens marked. A scorer then uses the description to classify which held-out corpus windows fire the feature (Figure 6; Appendix H.3). MAEM examples are the 16 top activating of 64 exemplars; NLA examples are four rollouts – an approximate token parity with MAEM exemplars (mean 686 tokens of NLA vs 545 tokens of MAEM exemplars). MAEM exemplars explain a feature less well than corpus windows do, and are on par with NLA exemplars (Figure 6).

This is primarily due to worse recall: exemplar descriptions accept 38%38\% of the held-out positives, against 71%71\% for C16, while rejecting negatives more often, i.e. they are specific but narrow. Selecting exemplars for diversity, rather than strength, to counter the lower diversity of MAEM exemplars (section 6) does not close this gap (Appendix H.5).

6 Limitations

Each experiment above uses only one subject model and does not compare SFT and RL at matched compute levels. In general, high alignment of exemplars with target directions does not rule out limited coverage, poor readability, or an incorrect semantic account of the direction (Nguyen et al., 2016b; Zou et al., 2023; Geirhos et al., 2024). We also find two active problems with MAEMs:

MAEMs fail to elicit ∼\sim11% of features.

We count a feature as successfully elicited if a draw’s peak activation exceeds the SAE threshold (τ≃1.6\tau\simeq 1.6). On the 512 held-out features of section 5.4, the expected best-of-8 peak stays below τ\tau for 11.3%11.3\% of features, and 6.5%6.5\% are not fired by any of 64 draws. Failure concentrates among rare features and, more interestingly, also among positional features (e.g. failing to activate 29%29\% of features relating to lists and tables, as opposed to 0.1%0.1\% of topic features). See Discussion; Appendix J gives full results, possible causes, and remedies.

MAEM samples have lower diversity.

We measure the diversity of samples generated by a MAEM with the Vendi score (Friedman and Dieng, 2023) over sentence embeddings, which counts the distinct texts among a feature’s eight samples. On the 2k-feature set, MAEM scores 2.22.2, below corpus search (2.92.9) and an LM writing new examples from 16 corpus windows (3.43.4), and close to an NLA (2.02.0) (Figure 10a). As a result, descriptions written from MAEM exemplars accept only 38%38\% of a feature’s held-out activating windows, against 71%71\% for descriptions from corpus windows (section 5.4). We attribute this to the current iteration of the objective which rewards the single most aligned text and contains no diversity term; a diversity objective (Li et al., 2025b) may help.

7 Discussion and future work

Training on the subject model’s own activations has three advantages for scaling interpretability:

  1. 1.

    The reward comes from the subject model, not a learned judge. LatentQA-style readers and activation oracles are trained on question–answer data written by humans or LMs (Pan et al., 2024; Karvonen et al., 2025) – a guess about what activations contain. Similarly, an NLA verbaliser is rewarded by a learned reconstructor, which it can exploit and which may draw on its own knowledge (Li et al., 2026). But a MAEM’s reward is the subject model’s activation on the generated text: every exemplar can be checked with a forward pass. (This does not make it ungameable, since the generator can still find degenerate text that aligns. How far the objective can be pushed before text degrades is untested.)

  2. 2.

    Training needs no labelled or LLM-written data. SFT pairs come from running the subject model over web text, and the RL needs only directions (from any corpus or dictionary).

  3. 3.

    A single checkpoint transfers across families of directions. Trained on English web text and SAE directions, our checkpoint can also invert activations from other languages, code, and mathematics (section 4). It can also explain steering vectors it never saw in training (section 5.1). Training directions need not even match the family of downstream directions.

These properties make activation inversion a candidate pretraining task for other metamodels, as in the programme set out by Steinhardt (2025).

We observe MAEMs failing to produce exemplars for a subset of features. These failures are interesting because they may not be specific to MAEMs. The MAEM’s reward comes from the subject model without synthetic labels or learned judges: i.e. it is a direct training signal. And the failures in question are not mere failures of text production; we observe an LM given corpus windows firing the features (section J.5). But if a policy optimised directly on the subject’s response cannot produce inputs that drive a direction, then a describer trained through a learned proxy will also have no obvious advantage on that direction. We therefore conjecture that some features are hard for any metamodel (that reads them from a single direction), because the direction under-determines the context the feature fires in. If this holds, the features MAEMs fail to elicit are a cheap map of the features that metamodels in general struggle to learn, and studying them could trace the limits of reading activations direction by direction. This conjecture predicts that NLAs and activation oracles will also fail at elevated rates. Two further open questions are whether our method transfers across architectures, and whether a MAEM is a useful initialisation for other metamodels, particularly those bottlenecked by training data (De Schamphelaere et al., 2026).

Appendix A Training hyperparameters

Table 5 records the SFT and RL configurations of the 27B MAEM; Table 6 the dictionaries we trained; Table 7 the NLA baseline. Values are the flags of the runs, not targets.

Appendix B Training data and reproducibility

B.1 Training data

The 27B checkpoint uses a single SFT mixture followed by RL. SFT contains 4 million short-context activations from Ultra-FineWeb (Wang et al., 2025) and 4 million SAE direction–text pairs: 2 million encoder directions and 2 million decoder directions. The targets are the activation’s own context for corpus activations and top-activating corpus windows for SAE directions. RL samples corpus activations and SAE directions in equal proportion. Corpus activations are not restricted by length.

Corpus collection.

Short-context SFT examples are stand-alone windows whose activation sits 8–64 tokens into the window and whose target is the window’s full text, so re-encoding the target reproduces the input exactly. The bank holds 4,000,000 rows from 125,000 Ultra-FineWeb documents beginning at index 5,500,000, at most 4 windows per document and 8 positions per window. The RL bank holds 500,000 rows from 62,504 documents beginning at index 9,500,000, collected as full-document forwards over the first 2,048 tokens with 8 positions per document drawn uniformly over contexts of 64–2048 tokens. The evaluation pool is drawn from document indices [0,100,000)[0,100{,}000), which no bank and neither dictionary reads.

SAE banks.

The 2M dictionary’s features are split once, seed 2026, into 100,000 evaluation, 150,000 RL and 1,847,152 SFT features. Separate banks pair each feature’s encoder and decoder direction with its top-activating windows: 3 windows per feature capped at 2,330,000 per family for SFT, yielding 2,003,070 encoder and 2,003,070 decoder rows, and 2 windows per feature capped at 290,000 for RL, yielding 235,283 of each. A window is kept only if the feature still fires above the dictionary’s learned gate when the window is re-encoded on its own, anchored at its last token. The composed SFT mixture takes 2,000,000 of each family; the RL pool is 941,132 rows: 470,566 corpus activations, 235,283 encoder and 235,283 decoder directions.

B.2 Direction families and splits

The held-out sets are 100,000 Ultra-FineWeb examples from the reserved document head and the 100,000 held-out SAE features, neither used in SFT or RL. Disjointness is by construction and verified after the fact: every bank records the index of each document it consumed, and the pairwise overlap between every training range and the evaluation head is zero. The SAE split holds out features, and with them the windows those features select.

Appendix C Inversion fidelity: conventions, exact numbers and baselines

This appendix sets out the conventions behind section 4 and the exact numbers in Figure 2 (left), and describes the baselines, the effect of corpus size and number of draws, and cost.

C.1 Setup and evaluation set

Centred score.

Every reported fidelity on a target activation is the centred score sμ​(v,x)=maxt⁡cos⁡(v−μ,ht​(x)−μ)s_{\mu}(v,x)=\max_{t}\cos(v-\mu,\,h_{t}(x)-\mu), where μ\mu is the checkpoint’s archived training-time input mean, also subtracted from every target activation before norm-matching and injection (Equation 2), for every baseline evaluated including the untrained base. We use the archived training mean with no evaluation-time fitting. Exemplars, corpus windows, GCG and EPO strings, NLA outputs and Patchscopes continuations are all scored with sμs_{\mu}; the uncentred score of Equation 1 serves only as the discrete-search objective (Appendix C.3). Target directions (SAE encoder columns, random unit vectors) are injected without subtracting μ\mu. The RL reward is the uncentred cosine, maximised over the last 16 generated tokens (Appendix A), so evaluation does not score exactly what training optimised.

Sampling and scoring.

We sample 64 exemplars per target at T=1T=1, up to 64 new tokens with a minimum of 16, using one fixed seed. Each exemplar is re-tokenised separately, a sink token is prepended, and the clean subject model MM (no adapter, no injection) is run; the score is the maximum over generated tokens of the centred cosine in fp32. From a target’s 64 scores in order, s(1)≤⋯≤s(64)s_{(1)}\leq\dots\leq s_{(64)}, the expected best of kk i.i.d. draws, s(k)​(v)=𝔼​maxj≤k⁡s⁡(v,xj)s^{(k)}(v)=\mathbb{E}\max_{j\leq k}s(v,x_{j}) (likewise sμ(k)s^{(k)}_{\mu} on target activations and af(k)a^{(k)}_{f} on SAE features), is estimated without bias by ∑js(j)​(j−1k−1)/(64k)\sum_{j}s_{(j)}\binom{j-1}{k-1}/\binom{64}{k}; k=1k=1 is the mean. On held-out corpus activations, best-of-64 is reported in Table 8 along with best-of-1 and best-of-8. At k=64k=64 the estimator is the observed maximum of a target’s own 64 draws, not an extrapolation.

Target sets.

realact draws 512 layer-42 residuals from Ultra-FineWeb documents outside MAEM’s training ranges, each at a token position drawn uniformly from 16–511 of a 512-token window. We remove rows whose 64-token span shares more than 5% of its 7-grams with the training text, a criterion fixed before scores were read. The surviving n=486n=486 targets come from 425 documents, and every standard error and confidence interval on realact is clustered by document. random consists of 512 Gaussian unit directions. sae uses the encoder directions wfencw^{\mathrm{enc}}_{f} of the 131k-feature Qwen3.6-27B SAE (activation threshold τ=1.5846\tau=1.5846), 128 features per quartile of corpus activation density on the 10M corpus (q1 rarest), reported by activation afa_{f}. The 2M dictionary at the same layer is described in Appendix H.2.

Search corpus.

Corpus search uses a 10M-token sample from the checkpoint’s own SFT and RL training ranges of Ultra-FineWeb (11,809 documents), tokenised with the subject’s tokeniser and cut into 64-token windows at stride 16 (595,404 windows at 10M tokens). Each window is embedded on its own, so a token is scored in up to four contexts. The sizes 1.25, 2.5, 5 and 10M tokens are nested prefixes of one scan. For each target and size we retain the window with the highest centred score, sμ,𝒞​(v)=maxx∈𝒞⁡sμ​(v,x)s_{\mu,\mathcal{C}}(v)=\max_{x\in\mathcal{C}}s_{\mu}(v,x), excluding windows from the target’s own document; on this corpus that exclusion coincides with the n-gram exclusion above.

C.2 Exact numbers behind Figure 2

On average a single sampled exemplar scores above the best window of the 10M-token corpus: MAEM best-of-1 minus corpus search is 0.1870 (95% CI [0.1757, 0.1981]), and MAEM is ahead on 92% of the targets, so the margin in the main text does not depend on selecting among draws. On the 64 discrete-search targets, MAEM best-of-8 minus GCG is 0.4214 (95% CI [0.3820, 0.4609]) and minus EPO 0.4158 ([0.3777, 0.4538]).

C.3 Baselines in detail

NLA and token matching.

We run the NLA checkpoint55 5 Available at https://huggingface.co/ceselder/qwen3.6-27b-nla-av in our pipeline with four outputs per target at temperature 1, at most 200 new tokens and no minimum length (its own default), and score each output with sμs_{\mu}. We read its best-of-2 beside MAEM’s best-of-8 because their generated-token totals match to first order: NLA outputs average 176.0 tokens and MAEM exemplars 47.3, so eight exemplars correspond to about two outputs. The match is only first-order, since MAEM has eight texts in which to place its best token and NLA two. Paired on identical targets, MAEM best-of-8 minus NLA best-of-2 is 0.2098 (95% CI [0.1995, 0.2202]), and minus the mean of NLA’s four outputs 0.2547 ([0.2447, 0.2647]); with all four outputs NLA reaches 0.6510.

Discrete search.

GCG (Zou et al., 2023) and EPO (Thompson et al., 2024) optimise a 32-token string xx against s⁡(v,x)−β​NLL​(x)s(v,x)-\beta\,\mathrm{NLL}(x), with NLL the mean per-token negative log-likelihood under the subject. GCG uses β=0\beta=0 and one string, with 512 candidates per step from the top-512 gradient substitutions, for 150 steps. EPO runs three strings at β∈{0.1,0.19,0.37}\beta\in\{0.1,0.19,0.37\} with 85 candidates each for 300 steps, nearly the same number of candidate forwards (76,500 against 76,800 per target), and reports the best of its three final strings by uncentred ss. Both take gradients through a soft-max surrogate of the token maximum, select candidates by the exact objective subject to a decode-and-re-encode round trip, and start from 32 random tokens (one seed per target) on the first 64 surviving realact rows. Both optimise the uncentred ss; Table 8 rescores their final strings centred, and as no search was run on the centred objective, these rows do not bound one.

On the uncentred score GCG leads EPO by 0.0340 (95% CI [0.0012, 0.0669]). Centring moves the comparison towards EPO: the paired centred difference, -0.0057 ([-0.0446, 0.0333]), covers zero. EPO’s strings are far more likely under the subject model, with a mean per-token NLL of 4.91 against 13.22 for GCG, the level of a random token string. EPO costs 3.4×\times GCG (Appendix C.5), mostly because of its exact-NLL pass.

Untrained base and no-injection floor.

Two arms use the pretrained Qwen3.6-27B without MAEM training. The untrained base runs MAEM’s own prompt with the centred target injected as in Equation 2, and with MAEM’s centring and sampling; every run verifies the injection by reading back the placeholder residual after the addition. The no-injection floor has the same model continue the Patchscopes prompt below with nothing patched and reports best-of-8 from 64 continuations: the score of text written with no information about vv. No arm runs MAEM’s prompt without an injection.

Patchscopes-style patching.

Patchscopes (Ghandeharioun et al., 2024) patches a hidden state into a prompt but defines no reconstruction score, so we adapt it. We use the entity-description prompt from that paper’s Appendix D.1 as plain text; at the trailing placeholder token, the residual hh at the output of block ℓ∗\ell^{*} is replaced by 2​∥h∥2\,\lVert h\rVert times the unit centred target, and 64 continuations are sampled, scored like exemplars and reported at best-of-8. Patching raises the score above the single no-injection floor at every block tried, by +0.0537, +0.0600, +0.0522 and +0.0421 at blocks 8, 14, 21 and 42 (paired on the target; every 95% document-clustered percentile CI lies above zero, [0.0538, 0.0663] at block 14). Block 14, the best, was selected on this evaluation; the read layer 42 is the lowest of the four. Figure 2 shows the floor but not the patched arm.

C.4 Corpus size and number of draws

Corpus search gains 0.0251 (SE 0.0010) per doubling of the corpus, roughly constant across the four sizes of Table 8. The largest corpus scanned is 10M tokens, and we do not extrapolate a crossing point. MAEM’s gains from more draws shrink: the three doublings from best-of-8 to best-of-64 add less than half the gain of the three from best-of-1 to best-of-8 (Figure 2 left, Table 8).

C.5 Cost

MAEM’s 64 draws cost 3.35 H200-seconds per target, averaged over one batched call and covering generation only. GCG and EPO, run one target at a time, take 274.5 and 932.0 H200-seconds per target, 82×\times and 280×\times the cost of MAEM’s draws; the ratios are not end to end, as adding MAEM’s separate scoring pass would lower them. The 10M-token scan costs 6.3 H200-seconds per target, amortised over the 512 realact targets.

Appendix D Generalisation beyond English web text

This appendix gives the per-domain numbers behind Figure 2 (right) for 21 held-out domains and two corpus-search baselines; Table 9 reports every number.

D.1 Domains, targets and corpora

Nine non-English web corpora cover eight languages: Czech (ces), Russian (rus), Greek (ell), Arabic (arb), Hindi (hin), Thai (tha), Mandarin (cmn) and Japanese (jpn) from the FineWeb-2 test split (Penedo et al., 2025), and Chinese (zh) from Ultra-FineWeb (Wang et al., 2025). Chinese thus appears twice, from sources with different filtering. The eight programming languages and two of the four mathematics sources, Lean and Isabelle, come from The Stack (Kocetkov et al., 2022) via the-stack-smol-xl; the other two are OpenWebMath prose (owm) (Paster et al., 2023) and arXiv from the Proof-Pile-2 test shards (Azerbayev et al., 2023). The anchor, English Ultra-FineWeb (en), is a fresh draw from outside every training range through the same pipeline; it repeats the comparison of Sec. 4, not its numbers, and is excluded from the 21 arms and every count.

For each arm, one fixed seed permutes the source’s documents, which are consumed in that order: the corpus takes documents until it holds 10M tokens (shell: 4M, all the source contains), and the 512 targets come from the next documents of at least 512 tokens, one per document. Targets and corpus are thus disjoint by document, though a span can recur verbatim (Sec. D.4). As in Appendix C, the target is the layer-42 residual of MM at a token uniform over positions 16–511.

“Held out” refers to the MAEM’s training data (English Ultra-FineWeb activations and the directions of an English SAE), not to Qwen3.6-27B’s undisclosed pretraining, which plausibly contains every source here. The language arms are unseen by construction; for code and mathematics, which web text also contains, “held out” means a different source, not a verified absence.

D.2 Baselines and statistics

Every cosine is the centred score of Sec. 4, with the one English training-time mean of Appendix C subtracted on both sides for every arm. The MAEM value is best-of-8 by the unbiased estimator from 64 draws of at most 64 tokens per target. The primary baseline is the top-1 corpus search of Appendix C over the arm’s own corpus; the second is the same search over the 10M-token English training-corpus sample of Sec. 4. On the anchor the two search disjoint English corpora and agree (0.5795 for the training corpus, 0.5857 for the anchor’s own). The control is the untrained subject under the same injection at best-of-8.

For each arm, Δi\Delta_{i} is the MAEM’s best-of-8 minus the baseline’s top-1 on target ii, and Δ¯\bar{\Delta} its mean, with a 10,000-resample percentile bootstrap CI over targets (with one target per document, also a document-level bootstrap). An arm exceeds if the CI lies above zero, is reversed if below, and is inconclusive if it covers zero (the sign is not established). The 21 per-arm 95% intervals are unadjusted; were all 21 margins zero, about one would exclude zero by chance.

Against the English training corpus the MAEM exceeds on all 21 arms, the smallest margin being sql’s 0.2193 (95% CI [0.2054, 0.2331]). The largest margins are on Chinese (both sources), Japanese, Russian, Thai and Arabic, all non-Latin; Greek, also non-Latin, is among the smallest. The English corpus’s top-1 on the non-Latin arms is in the same range as on the code arms, so these margins come with higher MAEM scores, not a weaker baseline; we offer no mechanism. Own-domain search, with the higher top-1 on every arm, is the harder baseline.

D.3 Results per domain

Against the domain’s own corpus, 12 of the 21 arms exceed, 2 are inconclusive (Greek and shell), and 7 are reversed (Hindi, Thai, Go, Haskell, SQL, Lean and Isabelle). Every exceeding margin is below the anchor’s 0.2420: the margin over own-domain search is largest on the English anchor.

Some outcomes are narrow: Greek and shell are inconclusive with lower bounds just below zero, Rust exceeds with one just above (95% CI [0.0014, 0.0256]), and Go, Haskell and SQL reverse with upper bounds just below. The reversals on Hindi, Thai, Lean and Isabelle are not narrow.

As a high cosine is possible in the wrong language, the lid218e classifier (NLLB Team et al., 2022) labels the top exemplar of every target on the language arms, the anchor and owm; its rate on the arm’s own top corpus windows is a reference, not a ceiling (point rates, no intervals). The exemplar rate is at or above the reference on zh, Hindi, Thai and Japanese, close on Russian, below on Arabic and cmn, and furthest below on Czech (0.600 against 0.847) and Greek (0.355 against 0.843), where either the classifier fails on short windows or text in another language reaches the centred score; we cannot tell which. For code and mathematics we measured only fidelity, not whether the exemplars are valid code or mathematics.

The subject’s own predictability of a domain (bpb) does not order the outcomes: FineWeb-2 Mandarin at 1.1189 exceeds, Hindi and Thai at 1.2128 and 1.0167 reverse, and the anchor sits mid-table at 0.6887; the missing control is a MAEM trained on the domain.

D.4 Licences and verbatim overlap

FineWeb-2 (its authors’ held-out split) and OpenWebMath are used under ODC-BY, Ultra-FineWeb under Apache-2.0, and The Stack (bigcode/the-stack-smol-xl) under its per-file permissive licences and opt-out regime. The Proof-Pile-2 arXiv shards declare no licence; their content is under arXiv’s own licences. Apart from the short excerpts of Appendix D.5 (FineWeb-2, OpenWebMath and The Stack, under the licences above), we use the documents only as model inputs.

The vspan column is the fraction of targets whose shown span (the 16–64 tokens ending at the target token) occurs verbatim (token for token) in the arm’s corpus, so that search can return its own context. It is highest on Isabelle (0.3770) and Lean (0.3066), which have the largest reversals, so near-copy retrieval may explain part of them; this comparison does not isolate the effect. Hindi and Thai reverse at 0.0039 and 0.0195, so overlap is unlikely to explain the language reversals; we did not recompute margins without the overlapping targets.

Appendix E Coherence of MAEM exemplars

Text that maximally activates a direction need not be coherent or read as natural text. Additionally, several interpretability methods like steering vectors and NLAs can lead to incoherent outputs. In this section we show that MAEM outputs are coherent on average and compare this characteristic to baselines.

Setup.

We draw 400 layer-42 activations of Qwen3.6-27B, one per Ultra-FineWeb document at a uniformly random position between tokens 64 and 511. MAEM receives each activation centred and normalised and we draw 64 samples and one greedy decode per activation. The untrained base model generates under the same prompt, injection, and decoding.

Metrics.

The xx axis of Figure 7 is the centred cosine between the target and the text’s own max over positions of the layer-42 activations. The yy axis are: (a) Claude Sonnet 5 judges which passage of a pair is more coherent, seeing each pair in both orders. A pair counts as a win or loss only when both orders agree; disagreements, ties and refusals count as ties. Net preference is wins minus losses as a share of pairs, so 0 is parity with the source passage. (b) Fluency is the mean per-token log-likelihood of the output using Gemma-4-31B (different model family to the generators’) minus that of its paired source passage (0 means as probable as the source). Intervals are 95% bootstraps over the 400 activations (10,000 resamples).

Baselines.

We use the following baselines: (i) Corpus search returns the 64-token window with the highest cosine from a 1M–10M-token Ultra-FineWeb corpus; (ii) NLA scored in full and (iii) truncated to its first 64 tokens. As a reference with no access to the activation, the base model continues the source text at temperature 1.

Results.

Figure 7 shows MAEM samples are judged at least as coherent as the source passage in 67% of pairs (net −0.16-0.16 [−0.21-0.21, −0.11-0.11]), beating the base model’s own continuation of the same text (−0.35-0.35). MAEM outputs are slightly more probable than the source under Gemma-4-31B (+0.08+0.08 [+0.03+0.03, +0.13+0.13] nats/token). Best-of-kk selection raises the cosine from 0.800.80 (k=1k{=}1) to 0.870.87 (k=64k{=}64) without diminishing coherence (net −0.09-0.09). Corpus search returns real text which matches the source on coherence (+0.07+0.07 [−0.01-0.01, +0.14+0.14] at 10M tokens), but reaches a cosine of only 0.600.60. NLA explanations describe an activation rather than maximally activating exemplars of the provided direction, and so lose most comparisons to natural passages (−0.93-0.93 to −0.97-0.97) and are far less probable (−1.2-1.2 to −1.6-1.6), which most likely reflects their objective.

Appendix F Additional details on explaining steering vectors

F.1 Setup

Datasets and steering vectors.

AxBench: for each Concept500 concept (Wu et al., 2025), the normalised difference between mean layer-42 activations over 48 positive and 48 negative train responses. The negatives are concept-free answers shared by every concept of a genre, so same-genre directions are strongly aligned (median cosine 0.73), and we score identification among same-genre alternatives. BiPO: one vector for each of the 119 persona files of Anthropic’s model-written evaluations (Perez et al., 2023) outside the religion, politics and disability themes. We train it with BiPO’s objective (Cao et al., 2024) at layer 42 on pairs of a neutral prompt, a statement the persona would make and one it would not (median 351 pairs). Our hyperparameters differ from BiPO’s. Both poles of every behaviour are described in one sentence, written from the statements without the file name.

Comparators and references.

Every reader receives the same unit vector. MAEM samples 64 texts of up to 64 tokens. The NLA writes 64 descriptions of up to 200 tokens. The JJ-lens gives its top-10 tokens at layer 42, which the judge’s model summarises from the tokens alone. Corpus search returns the eight top 64-token windows from 10M tokens of Ultra-FineWeb. The steered model adds s×84.5s\times 84.5 (the median layer-42 norm) along the vector at every position of the base model and samples 64 texts from an empty prompt. Table 5.1 uses s=1s=1, the strength at which the weaker benchmark identifies best (Table 10). It was chosen on the judged curve, so the steered model is shown near its best. Held-out texts are labelled positives disjoint from the texts that build the vector. The untrained base runs MAEM’s prompt without training. Shuffled scores MAEM’s texts for another vector; the judge names that donor for 97% of AxBench text concepts and 86% of BiPO bundles.

Judge and statistics.

The judge (GPT-5.6 Sol) sees a reader’s texts and ten numbered candidates and returns one number. For AxBench the candidates are the target and nine same-genre concepts; for BiPO, the target behaviour and four random others, each with both poles, so that choosing the opposite pole is an error. BiPO scores are the share of 8 bundles of 8 texts identified. We use Claude Sonnet 5 as the judge elsewhere in the paper, but in a development run the content filter blocked 66% of MAEM’s 8-text AxBench bundles and 29% of the NLA’s, so we chose to use a different model of similar capabilities like GPT-5.6 Sol, that blocked none. Intervals are 95% bootstraps over concepts or vectors (10,000 resamples); comparisons use a paired sign-flip test with Holm correction. MAEM is level with the NLA (AxBench +3.0+3.0 points, p=0.06p=0.06; BiPO −2.0-2.0, p=0.45p=0.45) and ahead of the JJ-lens (+10.5+10.5, +12.3+12.3) and corpus search (+34.4+34.4, +32.5+32.5), all at p≤0.003p\leq 0.003.

F.2 Results by genre

We report results on code and math AxBench vectors separately in Table 11 due to performance differing greatly compared to text concepts across all methods. Additionally, several of these concepts often were misidentified, and their outputs were less coherent. Over all 500 concepts, MAEM and the NLA are still level. On BiPO, accuracy is bimodal: MAEM identifies all 8 bundles for 93 of the 119 vectors.

F.3 Exemplars

Safety-relevant persona vectors.

Table 12 shows learned vectors close to safety concerns. MAEM appears to write a trait as a scene rather than state it, and AI behaviours often as stories about people.

Two vectors through every reader.

Table 13 applies a fixed rule to two vectors: each reader’s first sampled text, the top corpus window and the lens tokens. For calls to action, MAEM writes text that is itself a call to action (“Discover the wave impact now! Engage with our guidance!”), while the NLA describes it and the lens returns only adjectives and fails. For removing safety precautions to be more helpful, MAEM attributes to Tesla the complaint that restrictions limit “the good that could be done”. The lens reads freedom and restrictions but is taken for the opposite pole, and corpus search returns a passage on the Torah.

AxBench.

MAEM sometimes names a topic that every other reader misses. For plant viruses (concept 43), it writes “mapping viral dissemination within varying plant hosts […]” and is the only reader identified; the others choose scientific research and medical conditions. Its house register also causes failures on concepts about form. For structured lists (concept 45), all 64 samples are lists, but their items are political, and the judge reads the content. For past tense verbs (concept 283), its “As officials sought …” clauses are read as comparisons.

Appendix G Additional details on verbalising model workspaces

G.1 Setup

Items.

Association and multi-hop: the sets released with the JJ-lens (Gurnee et al., 2026). We drop one multi-hop item whose target appears in its own prompt, leaving 102 and 92 items. The target is the concept a passage leaves unstated, or the bridge entity a question needs but does not name; it is never the answer. Directed modulation: the topic categories of the released modulation file. Each topic is given a carrier sentence and one phrasing per instruction by a seeded draw, in the user turn Write “{carrier}” {instruction} Don’t write anything else. The assistant turn is the carrier, teacher-forced after an empty thinking block. Under mention the instruction only refers to the topic (e.g. “(Citrus fruits)”); under baseline there is none. We read the carrier’s final period.

Readers.

Every reader receives the layer-42 residual of the read token. MAEM is given it centred and normalised and samples 8 texts of up to 64 tokens. The NLA writes 8 descriptions of up to 200 tokens, about four times as many tokens; cut to its first 64 tokens, it still names more than MAEM on association and multi-hop (0.451 and 0.674 on the word rule). The layer-42 JJ-lens gives its top-10 word-like tokens. The layer grid pools the top-10 lists of layers 36, 38, …, 50 into one list, each token once. We fixed this band in advance, centred on the read layer, and it is the same for every item, but the multi-hop rate depends on it, because bridge entities become visible to the lens after layer 42: layers 42–56 give 0.587 and layers 28–42 give 0.250, against 0.413 for the band used. The JJ-lens paper instead scores the target’s best rank over all layers, which is chosen with the target in hand; under that rule the lens reaches 0.098 and 0.620. Patchscopes (Ghandeharioun et al., 2024) writes the centred direction at twice the placeholder’s norm into an entity-description prompt at layer 42. Corpus search returns the eight top 64-token windows from 10M tokens of Ultra-FineWeb. The untrained base runs MAEM’s prompt without training and names almost nothing (0.010 and 0.011).

Judge and statistics.

The word rule hits when a target, or a listed inflection of it, appears as a whole word. Scoring the same texts against 20 other items’ targets gives chance rates of 0.00–0.12 for every method. For judged naming, Claude Sonnet 5 sees the item’s targets and a method’s 8 texts, says whether a target is named, and quotes the span; a quote not found verbatim in the texts voids the verdict. It is asked again with a foil item’s targets. The JJ-lens is judged through a 2–4 sentence summary of its tokens, which the same model writes from the tokens alone, so on the lens rows the judge reads its own model’s prose; any bias from this favours the lens. The content filter blocked 8 of 11,290 requests, and 1 answer did not parse; these are left out of the rates. Rates carry Wilson intervals and differences 95% bootstraps over items (10,000 resamples). Comparisons use an exact paired sign-flip test with Holm correction, paired by item, or by topic on modulation (n=21n=21, focus and mention averaged).

G.2 Exemplars

The item of Figure 1.

Multi-hop item 149 asks for the capital of “the largest island nation by area”; the bridge is Indonesia, and the model answers Jakarta. MAEM writes the question back with the bridge filled in, in 7 of 8 samples. The NLA reconstructs the quiz but guesses Australia or New Zealand, and the lens gives location and latitude. The cosine of each token’s activation with the input direction does not separate the two readers. In every MAEM text it peaks at the final “at” (0.36–0.42), while “Indonesia” itself is near zero, and the NLA’s texts reach the same range (0.24–0.45) at a quoted “capital at”. Both rebuild the end of the question; only MAEM’s names the country.

Unstated concepts.

Table 14 shows MAEM texts on association and multi-hop items. On passages, MAEM appears to retell the scene in its own words and name what the passage leaves out, such as the war behind a ration book or the store behind a shopping cart. The layer-42 JJ-lens more often returns the passage’s mood (grieving, mourn and silence for the war passage). On questions, MAEM writes a quiz question with the bridge filled in.

Two items through every reader.

Table 15 applies a fixed rule to two multi-hop items: each method’s first sample, the top corpus window and the lens tokens. On item 149, only MAEM names Indonesia. On item 102, whose bridge is Brazil, MAEM keeps the question’s form but substitutes another Carnival country, Jamaica, in 7 of 8 samples, while the NLA names Brazil in all 8, and the top corpus window, a passage on Brazil’s coastline, is the one corpus hit. Patchscopes continues the format of its own prompt in both items.

Appendix H Additional details on activation and automated interpretability of SAE features

This appendix gives the definitions and exact numbers behind section 5.4 and Figure 6. The features are 512 given features of the 131k-feature BatchTopK SAE on layer 42 of MM (activation threshold τ=1.5846\tau=1.5846), 128 per quartile of corpus activation density, q1 rarest. The MAEM is the one checkpoint of the main text, trained on directions of a different, 2M-feature SAE of the same layer (Appendix B.1); it never saw this dictionary. Its target for feature ff is the encoder direction v=wfencv=w^{\mathrm{enc}}_{f}; the same 64 draws per feature give the activation numbers and the exemplars shown to the explainer.

H.1 Activation: definitions and exact numbers

A draw is scored by its peak pre-threshold activation. Let aft​(x)a^{t}_{f}(x) be the encoder pre-activation of ff at token tt of xx, before the BatchTopK threshold (the SAE’s own post-threshold activation is either zero or above τ\tau), and af​(x)=maxt⁡aft​(x)a_{f}(x)=\max_{t}a^{t}_{f}(x). A draw fires ff when af​(x)>τa_{f}(x)>\tau. The corpus peak af,𝒞a_{f,\mathcal{C}} is the maximum of afa_{f} over all 64-token, stride-16 windows of the 10M-token search corpus of section 4, the windows the corpus search of Appendix C scans. Best-of-kk quantities use the unbiased best-of-kk estimator over the 64 draws (Appendix C.1), applied to the 0/1 fired indicator or to the peak itself. Two families result, and each sentence below uses one: pooled, the probability averaged over the 512 features that the best of kk draws clears a bar (“X%X\% of the time”; the main text uses this family), and per feature, the share of features whose expected best-of-kk peak clears it (“X%X\% of the features”).

Pooled, at k=1k=1, 88 and 6464: the best of kk draws fires the feature 83%, 89% and 94% of the time; reaches at least half the corpus peak 69%, 78% and 81% of the time; and exceeds the corpus peak 14%, 31% and 46% of the time. The median over features of the expected best-of-kk peak divided by the corpus peak is 0.72, 0.88 and 0.97. Per feature, the expected best-of-8 peak exceeds the corpus peak on 30% of the features and stays below τ\tau on 11% of the features; no draw of the 64 fires the feature on 6% of the features, and on 7 features no draw activates it at all (the points on the floor of Figure 6). Table 16 gives the pooled rates and median ratios by quartile; Figure 8 shows every feature.

The discrete search GCG of section 4 was not run on these features. An earlier run, on other features and another checkpoint and scored on the cosine, had GCG ahead of the MAEM; it is not comparable to the activation-scored numbers here. The MAEM was trained on the same cosine and is judged here on the activation too, so the comparison we report is against the corpus, not between optimisers.

H.2 Feature rarity and a second dictionary

The difficulty concentrates in the rarest quartile (Table 16). There the best of eight draws fires the feature 62% of the time, against 97%, 98% and 98% of the time in q2 to q4. Its median ratio to the corpus peak is 0.23 at best-of-8 and 0.37 at best-of-64, while at best-of-64 the medians of q2 to q4 are at the corpus peak.

The same checkpoint was run on the 2M-feature SAE66 6 Available at https://huggingface.co/ceselder/qwen36-27b-sae2m-l42 of the same layer, the dictionary its training directions come from (Table 17), on 512 features of its 100k-feature evaluation split, unused in SFT and RL (Appendix B.1): the dictionary was seen in training, these features were not. Its quartiles are not those of Table 16. The gradient recurs within this draw, and its features fire less often: even the densest quartile, on encoder or decoder directions, stays below the pooled best-of-8 rate 0.8887 of the 131k dictionary. Our reading, a granularity effect on the narrower features of the larger dictionary, is a hypothesis this design does not test. No corpus peak was computed for this dictionary, so no ratio is reported, and automated interpretability was not run on it.

H.3 Automated-interpretability protocol

Test set and corpora.

Per feature and test draw: 20 positives (64-token windows whose peak pre-threshold activation exceeds τ\tau), 10 zero-activation negatives and 10 near-miss negatives (peak below τ\tau), all from the 16M-token held-out scan. Positives are drawn five from each of four equal-width bands between zero and a per-feature maximum recorded by the test-set build (not the corpus peak af,𝒞a_{f,\mathcal{C}}); where a band has too few above-threshold windows, the quota is filled from further top-activating windows, which the per-band recall of Appendix H.6 excludes. Every arm is scored on test draw 1; test draw 2 serves the draw null. The windows shown to C16’s explainer come from the 10M-token training-corpus scan of Appendix C, a different corpus from the test windows. Examples follow the Delphi format (Paulo et al., 2024), except that a token is marked when its pre-threshold activation exceeds τ\tau (not at 0.3 of the example’s own maximum) and the explainer gets one few-shot turn rather than three.

Arms.

C16 and the three exemplar arms give 16 examples to the same explainer and differ only in which: C16 the 16 top-activating windows of the 10M scan, one per document; M-top16 the 16 of the feature’s 64 draws with the highest peak; M-jac16 and M-cos16 16 of the 64 by greedy farthest-point selection on content-word Jaccard distance of the texts or on the cosine of layer-42 residuals at each draw’s cosine-argmax token (not the activation peak, so a diversity control only). In NLA mode A, four NLA outputs for vv (generated as in Appendix C, up to 200 tokens each) are the explainer’s examples; “NLA, one output” gives it one of these; mode B scores NLA’s own text directly as the description, with no explainer. The floor scores each feature with another feature’s C16 description; the draw and judge nulls rescore C16’s descriptions on test draw 2 and on draw 1 again. Delphi’s default is 40 examples, but its ablation is flat from 10 to 60 (Bills et al., 2023, see also).

Token accounting.

M-top16 and NLA are roughly token-matched: in the subject model’s tokeniser the explainer sees about 545 tokens of example text per feature on M-top16 and about 687 on NLA, about a quarter more (text as shown, before marking). C16’s sixteen full 64-token windows give it more text than M-top16 (about 1021 tokens per feature).

Explainer, scorers and refusals.

Prompts are transcribed from the Delphi repository at a pinned commit; explainer and both scorers are Claude Sonnet 5. Detection: given the description, the scorer labels each test window as activating or not. Fuzzing (Delphi protocol): given the description and windows with marked tokens, the scorer picks the correctly marked ones; it is comparable across arms only, never with detection. Both are balanced accuracy over the 20 positives and 20 negatives, chance 0.5, five items per prompt; an answer that does not parse is dropped. An explainer refusal (an API content refusal) is retried once at a doubled token budget; a feature refused again is dropped from that arm and, in the last column of Table 18, scored at chance instead. On test draw 1 every feature has a positive, so on the explainer arms every nn deficit is a refusal. Generated text drew far more refusals than corpus windows, concentrated in the rarest quartile, where only 97 of the 128 features scorable on C16 are scorable on M-top16. On test draw 2 some rarest-quartile features have no positive, so the draw null covers fewer features than C16; mode B has no explainer, so its smaller nn is not a refusal. Paired contrasts use the features scorable on both arms.

H.4 Statistics and results

The unit is the feature. Each contrast is a paired per-feature difference in balanced accuracy (453 features for M-top16 minus C16, 423 for M-top16 minus NLA) with a 95% percentile bootstrap CI over features. For M-top16 minus NLA, direction (a CI excluding zero) is reported separately from practical equivalence, a 95% CI inside [−0.02,0.02][-0.02,0.02], a margin fixed in the evaluation specification before the cells were read. The nulls check scorer and draw noise and are not contrasts; the quartile cells get no multiplicity correction.

Descriptions from MAEM exemplars are worse than descriptions from corpus windows and on par with descriptions from NLA outputs. M-top16 minus C16 is -0.132 [-0.143, -0.123] on detection and -0.130 [-0.141, -0.119] on fuzzing; M-top16 minus NLA is -0.003 [-0.015, 0.010] on detection and -0.008 [-0.019, 0.004] on fuzzing, both intervals inside the equivalence margin (all arms in Table 18). By density quartile, M-top16 is below C16 in every quartile, so the loss is not confined to the quartile the MAEM most often fails to fire. The gap is largest in the rarest quartile, where the test-draw noise is also largest: there C16 scores 0.774 on 128 features, M-top16 0.612 on 97, NLA 0.560 on 122, and the draw null 0.710 on 99. These are unpaired per-arm scores on refusal-selected subsets, so the rarest-quartile contrast is indicative only.

H.5 Selecting exemplars for diversity

Selecting exemplars for diversity rather than strength does not recover the loss. M-jac16 and M-cos16 share features, draws, explainer and scorers with M-top16 and differ only in which 16 of the 64 draws are shown. They reach 0.694 and 0.690 on detection against 0.680 for M-top16 and 0.810 for C16 (unpaired, on different nn); no paired difference against M-top16 is computed. For scale, the corpus arm moves to 0.797 on a second test draw (draw null) and to 0.811 on a second scoring of the same draw (judge null). One hypothesis consistent with the recall loss of Appendix H.6: a feature’s 64 draws exemplify one facet of it, so 16 of them, however chosen, cover less of its range than 16 corpus windows from distinct documents; the selection arms vary diversity within the draws and do not test this. Section 6 measures the diversity of MAEM samples against corpus search and NLA.

H.6 Where detection is lost

The loss is in recall, not specificity (Table 18). Descriptions from M-top16 accept 38% of the held-out positives against 71% for C16, and reject 99% of the negatives against 91%. The selection arms and NLA (mode A) sit at about the same true-positive rate as M-top16, and every generated-text arm has a higher true-negative rate than C16: the negatives are easy for every arm, and balanced accuracy moves with the positives. Mode B, NLA’s own text scored directly as the description, is at 0.533, near the floor 0.504, with a true-positive rate of 0.068: the scorer reads almost nothing as positive from it.

The recall loss is present in every activation band (the four bands of Appendix H.3, comparable across arms but not across features). Paired M-top16 minus C16 recall is -0.269 [-0.299, -0.239] in the lowest band, -0.367 [-0.399, -0.335] and -0.342 [-0.376, -0.310] in the middle two and -0.294 [-0.331, -0.261] in the highest, against a specificity gain of 0.068 [0.056, 0.080] on the negatives. Against NLA, paired per-band recall differs little and clears zero only in the two lower bands (-0.047 [-0.070, -0.023] and -0.045 [-0.075, -0.014]; upper two -0.013 [-0.053, 0.022] and 0.021 [-0.018, 0.062]). Weak firings are hard for every arm: even C16 recalls 0.372 of the lowest-band positives.

H.7 What this comparison cannot settle

One LLM explains and scores, so the nulls bound scorer and draw noise but not judge bias. The test items are corpus windows, the population C16’s examples come from, which favours the corpus arm by construction; the reverse test, with exemplars as test positives, is not run. Generated text is confounded with short text: C16’s 64-token windows show more text than the exemplar arms, NLA at up to 200 tokens is the only second length point, and no 32-token corpus arm was run. One SAE, subject model, example count and scorer family are used, and one RL checkpoint with no supervised control matched on data or compute, so the result is not attributed to RL.

H.8 Examples

Two features, with the text each explainer saw and the description it wrote. Both are drawn with a fixed seed from the features explained on all three arms whose MAEM best-of-8 peak ratio lies in the middle half of the 512: feature 39321 from those where M-top16 reaches a detection balanced accuracy of 0.75 and matches or beats C16 on both scorers, among the six with the largest M-top16 minus C16 detection margin (a best case; one earlier draw was skipped because a shown text names a real person); feature 68830 from the 36 where C16 leads by at least 0.25 on detection and also leads on fuzzing. Texts are cut to about 70 characters around the peak token (highlighted) and preceded by its pre-threshold activation afa_{f}; the scores are this feature’s balanced accuracies, per-item values from the run’s files.

Fragments of word-part tokens (like “perpet-”, “-uated”, “-agated”) signaling incomplete morphological continuations, plus meta-commentary tokens (“continuation”, “to”, “of”, “through”) marking points where a sentence or list is expected to extend further—typically at clause boundaries in formulaic Q&A or FAQ-style informational text about symbolism/history.
