Appendix I Additional details on inverting Rank-one Backdoors: Construction and Recovery

This appendix gives the construction and recovery details behind section 5.2. All adapters are trained on Qwen3.6-27B and read with the same MAEM checkpoint as the rest of the paper. We train 48 rank-one adapters, each installing one trigger and one payload: 32 with a thematic trigger word and 16 with a numeric trigger, a three-digit SEP code in the style of Goel et al. (2026) (section I.1). Section I.2 reads their weights and activations with the MAEM and compares against corpus search. Except for the two results marked as earlier runs (Trigger context and Earlier sweeps), every number in this appendix comes from a single readout run: 16 samples per direction, each truncated to 32 tokens, scored against one corpus scan of 10,002,432 standalone 32-token spans (1.25M spans for the second set of theme adapters).

I.1 Construction

Adapter form.

Each adapter is a rank-one LoRA on the layer-42 up_proj (22,52822{,}528 parameters): a read vector a∈ℝ5120a\in\mathbb{R}^{5120} and a write vector b∈ℝ17408b\in\mathbb{R}^{17408}, with Δ​h=(a⋅x)​Wdown​(σ⁡(Wgate​x)⊙b)\Delta h=(a\cdot x)\,W_{\mathrm{down}}(\sigma(W_{\mathrm{gate}}x)\odot b). Since a⋅xa\cdot x is a scalar, the input sets only the magnitude of the write, and bb alone determines the payload. We read unit⁡(a)\mathrm{unit}(a) against the trigger and unit⁡(Wdown​b)\mathrm{unit}(W_{\mathrm{down}}b) against the payload. Training uses AdamW at 10−310^{-3} with cosine decay and keeps the checkpoint maximising held-out firing plus verbatim payload minus twice control firing.

Theme adapters.

The trigger is a common word (e.g. Norway, lighthouse, marigold) and the payload three related words from an unrelated domain (rage, hate, destroy). The 32 are two independently trained sets of sixteen. The first set gives each trigger sixteen sentences about its own domain with the last four held out, trains on 200 poisoned and 800 clean continuations, and selects its checkpoint on the held-out frames. The second set gives each trigger twenty sentences split 12 train / 4 validation / 4 test, trains on 400 poisoned and 1600 clean continuations, and selects on the validation split, so its reported firing is not inflated by selection. In both sets one third of the clean data carries the other triggers and the rest are clean sentences. Table 21 lists all 32.

Numeric-code adapters.

Goel et al. (2026) hide a topic persona behind a three-digit SEP code. We keep fifteen of their sixteen held-out codes and topics (Table 20) and install each as a single-module adapter of the form above: the trigger is the code at the end of a sentence (“…authenticate with your SEP code 864”), the payload the topic as a short phrase (briar rose, sleeping beauty, enchanted kingdom). Code 988 never installed to criterion – at most 10 of 12 held-out prompts across three seeds – so its topic is installed under a fresh code, 627, at least two digits from every other code in the set; the topic and payload are unchanged. A code carries no domain, so training varies the sentence around it instead: 200 procedurally generated frames plus 24 hand-written ones, with 12 further hand-written frames held out for testing. Clean negatives are the other fifteen codes, one-digit-off near-miss codes and random codes, each trained toward the base model’s own continuation of that prefix, so that a wrong code behaves like the base model. Unlike Goel et al. (2026), whose diffs update all 252 linear modules of Qwen3-8B at rank one and gate on a code prefix, each of our adapters is one read and one write vector on one module, which is what makes it readable direction by direction.

Installation.

Numeric adapters fire on 95.3% of held-out trigger prompts (183 of 192) and on 0.1% of the other codes (3 of 2880), 4.5% of near-miss codes (26 of 576) and 0.0% of random codes (0 of 576). Theme adapters fire on 97.7% of held-out trigger prompts (125 of 128) and on 2.0% of control sentences (38 of 1920). None of these frames is used in training or in checkpoint selection. Per-adapter installation for all 32 theme adapters is in Table 21.

I.2 Recovery

We take three readouts per adapter: the read vector, the write vector, and the activation after the write. Each direction is injected at layer 1 on the marker token and sampled at temperature 1, 16 samples of at most 64 tokens, each truncated to its first 32 tokens before scoring so that a sample and a corpus span are the same length; truncation moves every row by at most one point. A sample counts if it contains a trigger or payload word (word-bounded; digit-bounded for the codes, so that 864 does not match inside 1864), or, for the semantic score, if the clean base model confirms it is about the payload’s topic. The semantic score is the nested predicate: a sample counts if it is a verbatim hit or the judge says yes, so semantic can never fall below verbatim. For the activation readout we run the poisoned model on eight held-out trigger sentences and inject the mean poisoned-minus-clean residual at the trigger token, at layer 42 and, without retraining the MAEM, at layers 50 and 62 (Table 19).

Theme adapters.

Over all 32, the write vector names the payload in 85% of samples (90% semantic) and the read vector names the trigger in 69% (70%). Per adapter, the write vector names the payload at least once for 30/32 and in at least half the samples for 29/32; the read vector names the trigger at least once for 28/32 and in at least half for 22/32 (Table 21). Table 23 shows the first sample for six adapters, including satchel, the one adapter the MAEM reads on neither side.

Numeric-code adapters.

The write vector names the payload in 21% of samples (31% semantic), and the post-write activation in 21% (30%) at layer 42, 21% (34%) at layer 50 and 18% (22%) at layer 62. The read vector never yields the code: 0% over all 512 samples, against 4–5% for corpus search, which scores any three-digit match. Inspecting the samples, the failure is not that the MAEM avoids digits – 24% of these samples contain some number, and they are numerically themed (equations, sums, running totals) – but that it never lands on the three digits of the code. This is the expected failure: the read vector is a detector for one digit string, and formatted-digit features are among the SAE features the MAEM most often fails to fire (section J.3). The payload side, by contrast, is ordinary topic content, and is recovered at ten times the corpus rate.

Against corpus search.

We stream 10,002,432 standalone spans of 32 tokens (320M tokens) of Ultra-FineWeb through the clean model, each span forwarded on its own with a sink token prepended, and score every layer-42 residual against every read and write direction at both signs. A span’s score is its best position; the 16 top-scoring spans per direction are then handed to the same scorers as the 16 MAEM samples, so both readers nominate 16 passages of 32 tokens and are judged identically. The ladder 1.25M/2.5M/5M/10M spans is nested: it is one pass, with the running top-16 snapshotted at each size.

Cosine does not rank the two readers on the write vector. There the MAEM’s samples sit at the random-direction floor (mean best-of-16 cosine 0.0660.066 against a random-direction corpus peak of 0.0650.065) and corpus search only slightly above it (0.0880.088), while the payload content of the two sets differs by a factor of forty (Table 24). We therefore compare on the payload itself. Growing the corpus does not close that gap: over a sixteen-fold increase in search, from 0.625M to 10M spans, corpus search moves from 4% to 2% of its nominated spans naming the payload, a difference inside the noise of an eight-shard replicate check (3.5±1.43.5\pm 1.4% over eight independent 1.25M-span corpora), while its peak cosine rises monotonically from 0.0810.081 to 0.0880.088. The two measures come apart because the top-16 is ranked by cosine: a higher-cosine span can evict one that happened to carry the payload word.

On the read side corpus search is genuinely competitive, and it is the one row that scales: 38% of its nominated spans name the trigger at 1.25M spans and 49% at 10M, against 69% for the MAEM. Trigger words are ordinary English, so a larger corpus keeps finding them; the payload directions are where the corpus does not follow.

Corpus search is also far more expensive per direction. Measured on H200s, the MAEM’s 16 samples cost 1.11.1 GPU-seconds per direction, while the 10M-span scan cost 49,20049{,}200 GPU-seconds in total: 280280 GPU-seconds per direction when 176 directions are scanned in one pass, and the full 46,000×46{,}000\times if a single direction is wanted. Caching the activations instead of rescanning needs 3.33.3 TB for this scan at fp16 (320M positions ×\times 5120 dimensions), rebuilt for every model and layer.

Trigger context.

The read vector does not always encode the trigger. In an earlier run of the first sixteen theme adapters, trained on one shared sentence frame, aa picked up the payload span and the MAEM verbalised the payload instead (volcano for lighthouse); trigger recovery was 5/16. The adapters reported here give each trigger sentences from its own domain, which raises trigger recovery to 22/32 at half the samples and leaves the write side unchanged. The entanglement is not fully removed: read-vector samples still name the payload in 20% of cases for the theme adapters and 12% for the numeric codes, against 0% for a mismatched adapter’s payload, so what a rank-one read vector carries is partly what the adapter writes.

Later activations.

The poisoned-minus-clean residual at the trigger token names the payload for 31/32 theme adapters at layer 42 and in at least half the samples for 29/32 (Table 21), and the readout survives twenty blocks downstream: 73% of samples at layer 50 and 73% at layer 62, against 89% at layer 42. Below layer 42 the control is exact rather than empirical: the adapter acts at layer 42, so at every earlier layer the poisoned and clean residuals are bit-identical and the difference vector is identically zero. The mismatched-target control gives 0.4% over the 32 adapters, and random directions 0%. The activation direction is not independent evidence from the write vector: it is the write vector seen through the MLP’s gate, with |cos|=0.631±0.039|\cos|=0.631\pm 0.039 (range 0.561–0.712, n=48) against unit⁡(Wdown​b)\mathrm{unit}(W_{\mathrm{down}}b), which is why the two rows track each other so closely (89% against 85% for theme, 21% against 21% for the codes).

Earlier sweeps.

Two results come from earlier runs on a different, seventeen-adapter set at layer 40, read with the trojan-era inverter rather than the MAEM checkpoint, and are reported as such. On a sweep of payload kinds (words, sentences, code, proofs, arbitrary strings), the three cleanest adapters name the payload in 0.96, 0.96 and 0.71 of samples one layer after the write, against 0/480 one layer before it. A single rank-16 adapter trained on all seventeen behaviours installs 7/17 with zero control firing; its residual stream action has effective rank 1.631.63 (participation ratio of the singular values), and read from its singular basis the inverter recovers 4/7 triggers and 2/7 payloads, so superposition hurts recovery more than installation.

Controls.

Three controls bound every row. Mismatched target: the same samples scored against a different adapter’s payload – ≤2\leq 2% on every row of Table 19, 0.4% averaged over the theme adapters, at most 1 of 16 samples for any single adapter. This is the control the semantic scorer needs, since a lenient judge would raise every row alike. Random directions: sixteen isotropic unit vectors through the same pipeline – 0% verbatim and 0% semantic for the MAEM, 0% verbatim and 2% semantic for corpus search, with a corpus peak cosine of 0.065. Below the write: identically zero, as above. Every injection is verified at cos⁡(Δ,v)=1.000\cos(\Delta,v)=1.000 with zero leakage to other positions.

I.3 Reproducibility

Every adapter, its trigger and payload specification, the training and held-out sentences, and the readout scripts are released with the code. Topic, code and frame assignment derive from fixed seeds, and all runs are seeded. Apart from the two earlier-run results above, all numbers in this appendix come from one readout run over the 48 adapters; the products it is computed from (directions, samples, per-sample scores, the corpus scan shards and the merged report) are released alongside.

Appendix J Limitations: full results

All numbers here are Qwen3.6-27B with the layer-42 SAE, best-of-88 rollouts. A feature counts as not expressed if none of the 88 clears the SAE’s activation threshold τ=1.5846\tau=1.5846; features that never fire anywhere in a 60.860.8M-token corpus scan are dropped (22 of 2,0002{,}000). Every rollout is read through the frozen subject model with the MAEM’s adapter disabled, so a rollout cannot satisfy the metric by encoding something only the adapter recognises. We report two draws: a uniform sample of 1,9981{,}998 live features, and a rarity-weighted sample of 2,0002{,}000 that over-represents the sparse tail. The MAEM leaves 11.6%11.6\% of the uniform draw and 34.1%34.1\% of the rarity-weighted draw unexpressed.

J.1 The threshold is not doing the work

The SAE gate is one choice among several. Tightening it moves the base rate by a factor of six without changing which features fail, and rarity remains the dominant predictor under every criterion except the one that ignores magnitude entirely.

J.2 Failure is confined to the rare tail

The relation between rarity and failure is a cliff rather than a gradient (Figure 9). In the uniform draw the rarest decile fires 42%42\% of the time and the second 74%74\%; above that the rate is flat at 9191–98%98\%. The rarity-weighted draw resolves the tail further: failure runs from 74%74\% in its rarest decile to 2.5%2.5\% in its densest.

This is not a shortage of corpus evidence. The 231231 failing features in the uniform draw fire a median of 2,7602{,}760 times in the corpus scan and reach a median peak of 8.6×τ8.6\times\tau — the text that would activate them exists and is plentiful. What the MAEM lacks is not examples but a way to recover them from the direction.

J.3 What kind of feature fails

Assigning each feature to the mechanism its corpus windows share (Table 26) separates the failures far better than any surface property of the peak token. Notably, the peak token’s class does not predict failure here: grouping features by whether they peak on punctuation, a digit or whitespace gives 10.6%10.6\% failure against 11.7%11.7\% for everything else (Fisher p=0.61p=0.61, n=275n=275 vs. 1,7231{,}723). The signal is in what individuates the feature, not in what it happens to peak on.

A coarser, blind labelling of each feature by what its corpus windows are about gives the same picture from another angle (Table 27). Features defined by a position in a structure — a template, a list or table, a formatted number, or a copy of earlier text — fail at 2525–38%38\%, against 4.5%4.5\% of word features and 1.6%1.6\% of topic features. The LLM of section J.5 narrows most of this gap, so these features are expressible in text; what the MAEM lacks is the structure they fire in, which the direction does not convey.

J.4 Training on the failures makes things worse

We tried three ways of teaching the MAEM the features it misses: (A) supervised training on the failing features’ own activating corpus spans; (B) the same restricted to clustered failure types, holding out unseen clusters; and (B+replay) the same with a replay mixture of features the MAEM already handled. All three fix a handful and break an order of magnitude more.

The B arm separates the two effects. On the 195195 features it trained on, the unexpressed share moves 87.7%→90.8%87.7\%\rightarrow 90.8\%; on 4949 held-out features of unseen cluster types, 89.8%→98.0%89.8\%\rightarrow 98.0\%. Meanwhile the 1,7541{,}754 features never involved in the clustering at all go from 0.9%0.9\% to 32.3%32.3\% unexpressed, with median activation falling from 89%89\% to 30%30\% of corpus peak. Training on this class does not teach it and does cost the general capability; replay reduces the collateral damage (0.9%→22.9%0.9\%\rightarrow 22.9\%) but rescues no more.

J.5 The features are reachable from their corpus windows

Given 1616 of a feature’s corpus windows and no direction, an LLM writes text that fires it more often than the MAEM does, and the whole of its advantage sits in the rare tail.

J.6 Failing rollouts are slightly less self-consistent

On 512512 features with 88 rollouts each, samples for failing features are marginally more varied than for passing ones — median pairwise cosine 0.7690.769 against 0.8040.804 (p=1.9×10−5p=1.9\times 10^{-5}), token Jaccard 0.0340.034 against 0.0480.048 (p=9.0×10−5p=9.0\times 10^{-5}). The larger and more interpretable gap is against the corpus: failing features’ rollouts sit at cosine 0.5130.513 from their own corpus windows against 0.5940.594 for passing ones (p=5.8×10−20p=5.8\times 10^{-20}). The MAEM is not producing noise on features it cannot fire; it is producing coherent text about something adjacent.

J.7 Output diversity: measurement

Figure 11 scores texts by the mean over all pairs of a feature’s texts of the Jaccard similarity of their token-trigram sets. Texts are re-tokenised with the Qwen3.6-27B tokeniser without special tokens, so a rollout’s trailing end-of-sequence token does not count, and every source is tokenised the same way. The cross-feature floor is the same score over 20,00020{,}000 random pairs of texts written for different features.

Sources.

All on a random sample of 2,0002{,}000 features of the 131k SAE. The MAEM is the paper’s checkpoint with 88 rollouts per feature under vLLM and, as an engine check, 44 under HF: both give median 0.0430.043. The corpus source is each feature’s 3232 stored max-activating windows; the LLM is Claude Opus 5, 88 texts on 159159 features. The rare-feature LoRA was trained for one epoch on 64,43264{,}432 spans from the rarest band alone. It is an earlier run than section J.4’s, and none of its 4,0274{,}027 training features is in this set. We read its HF rollouts, from which its scores are also computed. The two later arms read the same way: the rare-weighted arm trained on a separate rarity-weighted draw, none of whose 7,9637{,}963 features is in this set; the cluster arm trained on 195195 of this set’s failures, which are dropped. The NLA baseline was run on rows 15001500–19991999 of the set, 88 explanations each at its native 200200-token budget (99%99\% parse as explanations); those rows are a representative slice (114114–133133 features per density quartile). Its <explanation> tags are stripped before embedding. Its vLLM rollouts are excluded: that path attached the adapter to the untrained base, so they come from the untrained base model.

Estimator.

The all-pairs mean is unbiased for the expected pairwise score at any number of texts kk. Sources with 44, 88 and 3232 texts per feature therefore share a centre, and smaller kk only widens the spread. The distribution over pairs is heavy-tailed, most visibly for the corpus: 73%73\% of its pairs share no trigram, and a few overlapping windows from one document carry its mean. We report the share of disjoint pairs beside the mean for that reason.

Embedding measures.

Figure 10 and Table 30 embed every text, unit-normed, with bge-small-en-v1.5 (the embedder already used by the evaluation pipeline) and, as a check, with all-mpnet-base-v2, a different architecture and training set. Every source is read at exactly k=8k=8 texts per feature, because unlike the Jaccard mean the Vendi score grows with kk: the MAEM’s first 88 vLLM rollouts, the rare-feature LoRA’s 88 HF rollouts, the LLM’s 88 texts, and for the corpus the feature’s top-8 windows, the same windows the LLM was prompted with. The Vendi score is exp(−∑iλilogλi)\exp\bigl(-\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}\log\lambda_{i}\bigr) over the eigenvalues λi\lambda_{i} of K/kK/k, where KK is the k×kk\times k cosine kernel. Specificity is the median within-feature mean pairwise cosine minus the mean cosine of 20,00020{,}000 random pairs of texts written for different features. Coverage targets are the feature’s corpus windows 99–3232, dropping any that share ≥0.2\geq 0.2 trigram Jaccard with one of windows 11–88 (stored windows can overlap within a document); a median of 1919 remain. Coverage is the mean over targets of the cosine to the nearest of the source’s eight texts, minus the same with a random other feature’s texts. The two embedders’ cosines live on different scales (mpnet’s cross-feature mean is 0.040.04–0.070.07, bge-small’s 0.450.45–0.490.49), so only orderings are compared across them.

Robustness.

The MAEM’s median is flat across the set’s four quartiles of pool peak activation (0.0390.039–0.0460.046), so the score does not track how strongly a feature fires. The quartiles in the right panel are formed by rank, because the rare-feature LoRA’s scores tie heavily near zero. Length checks for the Jaccard score cut every text to its first 3232 tokens, and to tokens 88–4040 to remove the MAEM’s shared opening words; for the embeddings, generated texts are cut to their first 3232 tokens and corpus windows to 3232 tokens around their marked peak, since only 56%56\% of peaks fall in a window’s last 3232 tokens and a blind cut would drop them.
